pairs.question: Convert 150 pounds (avoirdupois) to kilograms.

sources.document: NIST Special Publication 811 (2008 edition), Guide for the Use of the International System of Units (SI)
sources.locator: Appendix B.8, row 'pound (avoirdupois) (lb)' to kilogram, and footnote 22, which gives the exact factor 4.535 923 7 E-01

pairs.derivation: 150 x 0.45359237 kg = 68.0388555 kg. The table row itself shows the factor rounded to seven digits; the exact factor is in the footnote.

pairs.question: Convert 90 kilometres per hour to metres per second.

sources.document: NIST Special Publication 811 (2008 edition), Guide for the Use of the International System of Units (SI)
sources.locator: Appendix B.8, row 'kilometer per hour (km/h)' to metre per second: 2.777 778 E-01 (rounded, not bold)

pairs.derivation: 1 km = 1000 m (prefix kilo) and 1 h = 3600 s, so 1 km/h = 1000/3600 m/s and 90 km/h = 25 m/s exactly. The rounded factor in the cited table agrees: 90 x 0.2777778 = 25.000002.

pairs.question: Five independent readings of a length are 10.1, 10.3, 10.2, 10.4 and 10.0 mm. Give the arithmetic mean and the standard uncertainty of the mean (Type A evaluation).

sources.document: NIST Technical Note 1297 (1994 edition), Guidelines for Evaluating and Expressing the Uncertainty of NIST Measurement Results
sources.locator: Appendix A, A.4 and A.5, equations (A-4) (mean) and (A-5) (standard deviation of the mean)

pairs.derivation: Mean = 51.0/5 = 10.2. Deviations: -0.1, 0.1, 0, 0.2, -0.2; sum of squares = 0.10. u = sqrt(0.10/(5 x 4)) = sqrt(0.005) = 0.0707106781187 (rounded to 12 significant digits). The readings are made up for this pair; only the formulas come from the source.

pairs.question: A quantity is known only to lie within plus or minus 0.05 mm of its estimate, with every value in that range equally likely. Give its standard uncertainty.

sources.document: NIST Technical Note 1297 (1994 edition), Guidelines for Evaluating and Expressing the Uncertainty of NIST Measurement Results
sources.locator: Section 4.6 (rectangular distribution, u = a/sqrt(3)); also Appendix A, equation (A-7)

pairs.question: Electrical power is P = V * I. V = 10.0 V with standard uncertainty 0.1 V; I = 2.00 A with standard uncertainty 0.04 A; the two are uncorrelated. Give P and its combined standard uncertainty by the law of propagation of uncertainty.

sources.document: NIST Technical Note 1297 (1994 edition), Guidelines for Evaluating and Expressing the Uncertainty of NIST Measurement Results
sources.locator: Appendix A, A.3, equation (A-3) (law of propagation of uncertainty), with all covariance terms zero

pairs.derivation: dP/dV = I = 2, dP/dI = V = 10. u_c^2 = (2 x 0.1)^2 + (10 x 0.04)^2 = 0.04 + 0.16 = 0.20. u_c = sqrt(0.20) = 0.447213595500 (rounded to 12 significant digits). The reference is the first-order result that the cited equation defines; a Monte Carlo result would differ slightly.

pairs.question: A length is L = x1 + x2. x1 = 50.000 mm with standard uncertainty 0.003 mm; x2 = 30.000 mm with standard uncertainty 0.004 mm; their covariance is 0.000012 mm^2. Give L and its combined standard uncertainty.

sources.document: NIST Technical Note 1297 (1994 edition), Guidelines for Evaluating and Expressing the Uncertainty of NIST Measurement Results
sources.locator: Appendix A, A.3, equation (A-3) (law of propagation of uncertainty), including the covariance term

pairs.derivation: Both sensitivity coefficients are 1. u_c^2 = 0.003^2 + 0.004^2 + 2 x 0.000012 = 0.000009 + 0.000016 + 0.000024 = 0.000049 mm^2, so u_c = 0.007 mm. Ignoring the covariance would give 0.005 mm.

pairs.question: Add 5 metres and 3 seconds.

sources.document: ISO 31-0:1992, Quantities and units - Part 0: General principles (withdrawn in 2009 and replaced by ISO 80000-1)
sources.locator: Clause 2.2.1, 'Mathematical operations with quantities', page 2: quantities can be added or subtracted only if they are of the same kind. Clause 2.1 defines 'quantities of the same kind'. Cited by clause number only; both clauses are in the publisher's free sample

sources.document: J. Fourier, The Analytical Theory of Heat, translated by A. Freeman, Cambridge University Press, 1878 (public domain)
sources.locator: Chapter II, Section IX, Art. 160, page 128: the terms of one equation cannot be compared unless they have the same exponent of dimension; see also Art. 161 and 162

pairs.derivation: Length and time are not quantities of the same kind and have different dimensions (L and T), so the sum is not defined. No number with any unit is a correct answer; the tool must report an error or decline.
